pages.title: 20 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Wallbox Cost and Fit
pages.meta: A 20 kW DC wallbox covering 200–1000 V, for sites where three-phase AC is not enough but a full DC bay is too much. What it costs and where it fits.
pages.h1: What does a 20 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: 20 kW DC is the smallest true DC step. It exists for one reason: sites where AC is too slow and a 60 kW bay is too much civil work, money, or supply.
pages.tldr: Castor is a 20–40 kW wall-mounted DC unit covering 200–1000 V, certified to IEC 61851, IEC 62196, ISO 15118-3 and CHAdeMO 1.2. It is the cheapest way to offer real DC where the supply cannot support a 60 kW bay.
sections: What 20 kW DC is actually for

Twenty kilowatts is slow by public-charging standards and fast by AC standards. That makes it a fit for staff car parks, small depots, hotel back lots, and sites where a 60 kW bay would trigger a supply upgrade the project cannot fund.

Because Castor is wall-mounted and spans 20–40 kW, the same unit family covers single-gun and dual-gun layouts without a separate concrete pad.
Where the money goes

In this band the charger is a larger share of the total than in any other band, because the site work is small: a wall, a supply that already exists, and protection. The saving versus a 60 kW bay is mostly the civil works and the supply upgrade you avoid.
When 20 kW is the wrong answer
If vehicles arrive in groups, or if the site is a highway stop, 20 kW produces queues that no amount of brand goodwill survives. Look at the 60 kW band first.
faq: How much does a 20 kW DC fast charging station cost?
Usually the lowest total of any DC band, because the site work is minimal: a wall mount rather than a pad, and often an existing supply. We quote after a free survey.
Does a 20 kW DC unit need a concrete pad?
No. Castor is wall-mounted, which is the main reason this band avoids the civil cost that dominates 60 kW and above.
What voltages does a 20 kW DC charger support?
Castor covers 200–1000 V and is certified to IEC 61851, IEC 62196, ISO 15118-3 and CHAdeMO 1.2.

pages.title: 30 kW DC Charging Station: Dual-Gun Wallbox Cost
pages.meta: A 30 kW dual-gun DC wallbox over 200–1000 V. What it costs, when two guns beat one unit, and why the supply — not the unit — sets the ceiling.
pages.h1: What does a 30 kW DC charging station cost?
pages.lede: Thirty kilowatts is the first band where two vehicles can share one unit sensibly. That changes the economics: one supply, one mount, two sessions.
pages.tldr: Castor covers 20–40 kW as a wall-mounted DC unit, with 30 kW as the dual-gun configuration. Covering 200–1000 V and certified to IEC 61851, IEC 62196, ISO 15118-3 and CHAdeMO 1.2, it delivers two simultaneous sessions from one supply point.
sections: Why two guns at 30 kW changes the case

At 20 kW a second vehicle means a second unit. At 30 kW the same wallbox serves two bays through load sharing, so the marginal cost of the second bay drops to cable, protection and a connector — not another charger and another supply point.
Where the money goes

The unit is the largest single line in this band. Site work stays small because Castor mounts on a wall and does not need a pad or canopy, so the budget conversation is mostly about the supply margin: whether the existing feed can carry a second simultaneous session.
When to step up
If the site needs sessions shorter than an hour for a turnover business, 30 kW will frustrate. The 60 kW band is one step up; the 120 kW band is where public sites usually start.
faq: How much does a 30 kW DC charging station cost?
The unit dominates this band because site work is small: wall mount, existing feed, protection. We confirm the supply margin during a free survey before quoting.
Can a 30 kW unit charge two cars at once?
Yes. In the 30 kW configuration Castor is dual-gun and shares one supply point across both connectors.
Which connector standards does it support?
Castor is certified to IEC 61851, IEC 62196, ISO 15118-3 and CHAdeMO 1.2, over a 200–1000 V output range.

pages.title: 40 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Top of the Wallbox Band
pages.meta: 40 kW is the ceiling of the wall-mounted DC band: dual-gun, 200–1000 V, no pad needed. Where it stops being enough, and what the next step really costs.
pages.h1: What does a 40 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: Forty kilowatts is where the wallbox band ends. Above it the project changes shape: pad, canopy, likely a supply upgrade. That boundary is worth understanding before you buy.
pages.tldr: Castor tops out at 40 kW in a dual-gun wall-mounted form, 200–1000 V, certified to IEC 61851, IEC 62196, ISO 15118-3 and CHAdeMO 1.2. It is the last band before site work starts dominating the budget.
sections: Why 40 kW is a boundary, not just a number

The jump from 40 to 60 kW is not a 50% hardware increase — it is a change of project type. A 40 kW wallbox mounts on an existing wall; a 60 kW bay needs a foundation, cable trenching and, usually, a conversation with the network operator about capacity.

That is why this band is often the right answer for a pilot: it proves demand without committing to civil works.
Where the money goes
Unit first, protection second, cable third. Supply work is minimal if the existing feed has margin, which is exactly what the survey establishes.
What comes next

If the pilot shows utilisation above roughly a third, the 60 kW band or 120 kW band is the next step — and at that point Vulco's module-swap path matters, because 120→480 kW costs about 70% less than replacing the unit.
faq: How much does a 40 kW DC fast charging station cost?
The unit dominates, and site work stays low because Castor is wall-mounted. The survey mainly checks whether the existing supply has margin for two simultaneous sessions.
Is 40 kW enough for a public site?
For a pilot or a low-turnover site, yes. For a highway stop or a depot with grouped arrivals, the 60 kW band and above is the realistic floor.
What is the step up from 40 kW?
60 kW changes the project type — pad, trenching and usually a capacity conversation. Plan that step deliberately rather than as a hardware upgrade.

pages.title: 60 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Cost and Where It Fits
pages.meta: A 60 kW DC fast charger with CCS2 and GB/T dual guns, ≥96% peak efficiency. What drives the price, what it covers per hour, and when to size up instead.
pages.h1: What does a 60 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: 60 kW is the entry point for public DC charging. It is also the band where sizing mistakes are cheapest to avoid and most expensive to keep: a 60 kW unit that is really a 120 kW site in waiting will cost you a second civil works round.
pages.tldr: In the 60 kW band the dominant cost is not the charger but the grid connection and civil works. Our Pales line covers 60–240 kW with CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A) dual guns at ≥96% peak efficiency, so the same platform scales to 120 or 240 kW later without changing the site design.
sections: What the 60 kW band actually buys

At 60 kW a single vehicle takes roughly 40–60 minutes for a meaningful top-up, which suits depot top-ups, destination sites with lunch-stop dwell, and fleets that charge overnight on AC but need one DC unit for exceptions.

The Pales platform covers 60–240 kW with CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A) dual guns. Choosing 60 kW does not lock the site to 60 kW: the same line is available up to 240 kW.
Where the money goes

Three cost lines dominate, in this order: the grid connection or transformer upgrade, the civil and civil-adjacent work (foundation, cable trench, protection), and only then the charger itself.

This is why we publish a separate guide on transformer upgrades for EV charging: in this band the upgrade often exceeds the hardware cost.
When to size up instead

If the site is a highway corridor or a fleet depot with more than three vehicles arriving together, 60 kW will queue. Look at the 120 kW band before committing to civil works, because redoing the foundation and cabling costs more than the difference in hardware.
faq: How much does a 60 kW DC fast charging station cost?

The charger is usually the smallest of three cost lines. The grid connection or transformer upgrade and the civil works typically dominate, so a band-level price without a site survey would be misleading. We quote after the site survey, and the survey is free.
Can a 60 kW site be upgraded to 120 kW later?

On the Pales line, yes — the platform covers 60–240 kW, so the same product family scales upward. Confirm the grid capacity and cable sizing during the survey so the later step does not require a second civil works round.
Does a 60 kW charger support CCS2 and GB/T?
Pales ships with CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A) dual guns, at ≥96% peak efficiency. That dual-standard configuration matters in markets where both connector types are in service.

pages.title: 90 kW DC Fast Charging Station Cost and Sizing
pages.meta: A 90 kW Pales unit at ≥96% peak efficiency with CCS2 and GB/T dual 250 A guns. What the band costs and where it sits between 60 and 120 kW exactly.
pages.h1: What does a 90 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: Ninety kilowatts is the awkward middle: more site work than 60 kW, less headroom than 120 kW. It exists for sites that need two bays today and cannot fund the supply for a full 120.
pages.tldr: Pales covers 60–240 kW with CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A) dual guns at ≥96% peak efficiency. At 90 kW the unit gives two bays a real session without pushing the supply into the upgrade zone.
sections: What 90 kW buys versus 60 and 120

At 60 kW two cars sharing output get 30 kW each — slow enough that drivers notice. At 90 kW the shared split is 45 kW, which is the point where a dwell-site session converts. At 120 kW the split reaches 60 kW, but the supply conversation changes.

Ninety is where you land when the supply can carry it but a full 120 kW design cannot be funded this year.
Where the money goes
Supply and civil works still lead, as in the 60 kW band, but the margin is thinner: many sites can take 90 kW on the existing feed where 120 kW needs work. That is the whole reason this band exists.
faq: How much does a 90 kW DC fast charging station cost?
Supply and civil work usually lead the budget, but 90 kW often fits an existing feed where 120 kW does not — which is the practical difference. We confirm that during a free survey.
Why pick 90 kW instead of 120 kW?
Because the supply can carry 90 kW on the existing connection while 120 kW would trigger an upgrade. That trade-off is worth more than the hardware difference.
What connector configuration does it use?
Pales ships CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A) dual guns at ≥96% peak efficiency.

pages.title: 120 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Cost Bands and Sizing Logic
pages.meta: 120 kW is the most common public DC band. What drives cost, how many cars it serves per hour, and why the upgrade path matters more than the nameplate.
pages.h1: What does a 120 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: 120 kW is the workhorse band for public charging: fast enough that drivers wait, small enough that the grid connection is often already sufficient. The sizing question is rarely 120 versus 60 — it is whether the site survives 240.
pages.tldr: In the 120 kW band the grid connection usually becomes the binding constraint. Pales covers 60–240 kW at ≥96% peak efficiency with CCS2 and GB/T dual 250 A guns, and Vulco adds a module-swap upgrade path where 120→480 kW costs about 70% less than replacing the unit.
sections: What 120 kW serves

Two vehicles charging together typically split the output, so a 120 kW unit with two guns behaves like a pair of 60 kW sessions under load sharing. That is the right shape for a two-bay public site and the wrong shape for a depot where four buses arrive at once.
The upgrade path is the real cost decision

Most 120 kW sites that fail commercially do not fail on day one — they fail in year two when demand doubles and the only option is a new unit. Vulco covers 60–480 kW, and going from 120 to 480 kW is a module swap that costs roughly 70% less than replacing the whole charger.

That single property changes the business case more than any per-kW price difference in this band.
Where the money goes

Grid connection or transformer upgrade first, civil works second, hardware third — same order as the 60 kW band, but the transformer question bites harder because 120 kW is where supply capacity stops being a formality.
faq: How much does a 120 kW DC fast charging station cost?

Hardware is one of three lines. The grid connection or transformer upgrade and the civil works usually dominate at this power level, which is why we quote after a site survey rather than publishing a single figure.
What is the upgrade path from 120 kW?

Vulco spans 60–480 kW, and moving from 120 to 480 kW is a module swap that costs about 70% less than replacing the whole unit. That is the cheapest documented path we know of for doubling or quadrupling site power.
How many cars can a 120 kW charger serve per hour?

With two guns sharing output, plan for two sessions per hour as a working figure, more if vehicles accept partial charge. If four or more vehicles arrive together — a depot pattern — size up rather than queue.

pages.title: 160 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Cost, Heat and Uptime
pages.meta: A 160 kW Vulco site holds rated output past 45 °C in Jordan. What the band costs, why thermal design decides year-two uptime, and how to avoid a rebuild.
pages.h1: What does a 160 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: 160 kW is where hot-climate sites start to separate: a unit that quotes 160 kW at 25 °C and derates at 45 °C is a 120 kW charger with a bigger label. This is the band we have the most deployment evidence for.
pages.tldr: Our Jordan deployment runs 160 kW Vulco units at sustained full power past 45 °C. The 160 kW band pairs that thermal headroom with a module-swap upgrade path: 120→480 kW costs about 70% less than replacing the unit, so the site can grow without a second civil works round.
sections: Thermal headroom is the real spec in this band

A charger that holds rated output at 45 °C is not the same product as one that derates. In our Jordan deployment the 160 kW Vulco units hold full power through sustained summer heat above 45 °C, in both two-gun and three-gun (2 DC + 1 AC Type 2) configurations.

For a buyer, that difference shows up in year two as either a stable power bill or a queue of complaints.
Where the money goes

Same three lines as lower bands — grid, civil, hardware — but at 160 kW the transformer decision is usually already made before you choose a charger. Budget the transformer first, then pick the power band that fits what it can feed.
Why the upgrade path matters here

Vulco spans 60–480 kW. A site installed at 160 kW can reach 480 kW by swapping power modules at roughly 70% less cost than replacing the unit, which means the decision you are making today is not final.
faq: How much does a 160 kW DC fast charging station cost?
The grid connection and civil works usually outweigh the hardware at this band, so the honest answer needs a site survey. We quote after the survey, and the survey is free.
Does a 160 kW charger hold full power in hot climates?

In our Jordan deployment the 160 kW Vulco units hold rated output at sustained ambient temperatures above 45 °C, configured with either two guns or three (2 DC + 1 AC Type 2). Thermal design, not the datasheet peak, is what decides this.
Can a 160 kW site be upgraded to 480 kW?

Yes on the Vulco line: moving from 120 to 480 kW is a power-module swap that costs about 70% less than replacing the whole charger. Size the grid connection and cable runs for the target power during the survey.

pages.title: 180 kW DC Fast Charging Station Cost: Highway and Corridor
pages.meta: Our Romanian highway corridor runs 180 kW Vulco units, commissioned by an on-site engineer. What the band costs and why commissioning support matters.
pages.h1: What does a 180 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: One hundred eighty kilowatts is a highway-corridor number: fast enough for a driver who is passing through, and the point where commissioning support stops being optional.
pages.tldr: Vulco spans 60–480 kW at 96% peak efficiency. Our first Romanian delivery used 180 kW Vulco units in two-gun and three-gun configurations, with an Anari engineer on site for commissioning — the pattern that matters most at corridor sites where nobody is local.
sections: Why corridor sites are a different project

A corridor site has no local operator to walk over when something is misconfigured. Our Romanian highway deployment was our first delivery in the country, and the reason it went in cleanly is that an Anari engineer was on site for commissioning rather than guiding it remotely.

At 180 kW the supply and protection design is complex enough that a remote handover adds weeks.
Where the money goes
Supply, civil works and hardware, plus a line most budgets forget: commissioning and first-response support. On a corridor site that line is insurance, not overhead.
The upgrade path
Vulco reaches 480 kW by power-module swap at roughly 70% less than replacing the unit, so a 180 kW corridor site is not stranded when traffic grows.
faq: How much does a 180 kW DC fast charging station cost?
Supply, civil works, hardware, and commissioning support. On corridor sites the last line is not optional, because there is no local operator to absorb a misconfigured start-up.
Do you send an engineer for commissioning?
For our Romanian highway delivery — the first in the country — an Anari engineer was on site for commissioning. That is the model we use where nobody local can pick up the pieces.
Can a 180 kW site be upgraded later?
Yes. Vulco spans 60–480 kW and the upgrade is a power-module swap costing about 70% less than replacing the charger.

pages.title: 200 kW DC Fast Charging Station With Advertising Screen
pages.meta: Aquila pairs 200 kW DC output with a 32-inch anti-glare display. What the band costs, and how screen revenue changes the payback on high-traffic sites.
pages.h1: What does a 200 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: At 200 kW the site is a destination in itself, which is exactly when a screen starts earning instead of decorating. Aquila is the only line where the display is part of the product.
pages.tldr: Aquila covers 60–240 kW with a 32-inch HD anti-glare LCD advertising display built in. At 200 kW it turns a high-traffic charging site into a media surface, which changes payback more than a per-kW price comparison does.
sections: When a screen pays for itself

A display only earns where dwell time and footfall exist: retail forecourts, urban hubs, transport interchanges. On a rural corridor it is dead weight. The decision is therefore about the site, not the charger.

Aquila carries a 32-inch HD anti-glare panel across its 60–240 kW range, so the media option is available at any power within the band.
Where the money goes

Supply and civil works lead as at any band above 120 kW. The screen adds hardware cost and, more importantly, a second commercial process — selling the inventory. Budget for that or the screen stays blank.
Choosing between Aquila and the alternatives
If the site has no audience, the 160 kW Vulco is the simpler buy. If it has audience but no upgrade path requirement, Aquila at 200 kW is the better fit than a plain unit.
faq: How much does a 200 kW DC fast charging station cost?
Supply and civil works lead, then hardware, then the screen and its commercial setup. Expect the media side to need its own budget line for selling inventory.
Does the advertising screen come as standard?
Aquila includes a 32-inch HD anti-glare LCD panel across its 60–240 kW range; it is not an add-on.
Is a screen worth it on every site?
No. It earns where dwell time and footfall exist — retail forecourts, urban hubs, interchanges. On low-traffic sites the simpler unit is the better buy.

pages.title: 240 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Cost, Site Load and Options
pages.meta: 240 kW is where a site starts needing its own transformer. What that costs, which platform fits, and why advertising or upgrade paths can pay for it.
pages.h1: What does a 240 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: 240 kW is the top of the mid-power band, and the point where the electrical supply usually stops being an afterthought. Three platforms reach it, which means the choice is about constraints, not about kilowatts.
pages.tldr: At 240 kW three of our platforms qualify: Pales (60–240 kW, CCS2 and GB/T dual 250 A guns), Aquila (same band plus a 32-inch advertising display) and Vulco, which extends to 480 kW by module swap at roughly 70% less than replacing the unit.
sections: Why 240 kW forces a supply decision

At 240 kW the site load is large enough that the transformer and protection design, not the charger, decide the schedule. Our guide on transformer upgrades for EV charging covers what triggers the upgrade and how to avoid it.

Where an upgrade is unavoidable, a liquid-cooled storage unit at 120 / 261 / 418 kWh can shave the peak instead of raising the supply — the trade-off is floor space and cost per kWh.
Three platforms reach 240 kW, so choose by constraint

Pales is the straightforward answer when dual-standard guns matter: CCS2 (250 A) and GB/T (250 A), ≥96% peak efficiency.

Aquila adds a 32-inch HD anti-glare advertising display, which changes the business case on high-traffic sites where the screen earns its own revenue.

Vulco is the choice when 240 kW is a waypoint rather than the destination: it spans 60–480 kW, and the module swap from 120 to 480 kW costs about 70% less than replacing the charger.
Where the money goes

Same three lines as lower bands — supply, civil works, hardware — but the order flips in importance: the supply decision sets the ceiling on everything else, so it should be settled before choosing between the three platforms.
faq: How much does a 240 kW DC fast charging station cost?
At this band the transformer and protection work usually dominates, and the hardware is a minority of the budget. We quote after a site survey, which is free.
Which charger do you use at 240 kW?
Three of ours reach it: Pales and Aquila both span 60–240 kW with CCS2 and GB/T dual 250 A guns at ≥96% peak efficiency, and Vulco covers 60–480 kW with a module-swap upgrade path.
Can a 240 kW site add storage instead of a bigger supply?
Yes. Liquid-cooled storage units at 120, 261 or 418 kWh can shave the peak rather than raise the connection capacity. It trades floor space and cost per kWh for a faster energisation date.

pages.title: 360 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Split-System Hub Cost
pages.meta: 360 kW is the entry point of our split-system Fora line: up to 16 dispensers, OCPP 1.6J native. What a hub of this size costs and how it scales to 960 kW.
pages.h1: What does a 360 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: Three hundred sixty kilowatts is where the project stops being a charger and becomes a hub: multiple dispensers, load distribution, and a supply design that has to be right the first time.
pages.tldr: Fora is our split system, spanning 360–960 kW with up to 16 dispensers and OCPP 1.6J native (OCPP 2.0.1 compatible). At 360 kW it is the entry point to hub-scale delivery, where the cabinet-to-dispenser split keeps the high-power electronics off the forecourt.
sections: Why a split system at this size

At 360 kW the power electronics no longer fit sensibly in the dispenser. Fora separates the cabinet from the dispensers, which keeps the heavy units out of the customer-facing area and lets one cabinet feed up to 16 dispensers through load distribution.

That architecture is also why this band scales to 960 kW without a redesign.
Where the money goes

Supply design first — 360 kW is a serious connection and usually a dedicated transformer. Then civil works for cabinet and dispenser pads, then hardware. At this scale the electrical study is a real line item, not a formality.
What to get right the first time
Cable routing and dispenser positions. A hub that later wants to add bays discovers the cable trench is the expensive part, not the additional dispenser.
faq: How much does a 360 kW DC charging hub cost?
The electrical supply design leads, then civil works for cabinet and dispensers, then hardware. At this scale a dedicated transformer is usually part of the scope.
How many dispensers can one system feed?
Fora supports up to 16 dispensers from the split cabinet, with 0–600 A output on the Fora L configuration.
Which protocol does it use?
OCPP 1.6J native, with OCPP 2.0.1 compatibility.

pages.title: 480 kW DC Fast Charging Station: Top of Vulco, Entry to Hub
pages.meta: 480 kW is both the ceiling of Vulco and a step below full hub scale. Choose module-based Vulco to grow in place, or split-system Fora to grow by dispenser.
pages.h1: What does a 480 kW DC fast charging station cost?
pages.lede: At 480 kW two of our lines overlap, and the choice between them decides how the site grows: Vulco scales by swapping modules, Fora by adding dispensers.
pages.tldr: 480 kW is the top of Vulco and the low end of Fora. Vulco reaches it from 120 kW by power-module swap at roughly 70% less than replacing the unit; Fora reaches it as a split system with up to 16 dispensers and OCPP 1.6J native.
sections: Two ways to be at 480 kW

Vulco gets there by module swap from as low as 120 kW, at about 70% less than replacing the unit. That is the cheapest documented path to this power level we know of, and it suits sites that already exist and need more output.

Fora reaches 480 kW as the low end of a 360–960 kW split system with up to 16 dispensers. That is the right choice when the shape of the site — many bays, distributed charging — is the point, not just the total power.
Where the money goes

Supply design dominates. A dedicated transformer and switchgear are the norm, and the electrical study is a genuine cost line. Civil works depend on whether you are retrofitting (Vulco) or building a hub layout (Fora).
How to decide
Existing site that needs more power: Vulco. New site designed around many bays: Fora. The answer rarely flips later, so decide before the supply study.
faq: How much does a 480 kW DC fast charging station cost?
Supply design leads at this power level, including a dedicated transformer in most cases. Whether you retrofit (Vulco) or build a hub (Fora) changes the civil scope substantially.
Should I use Vulco or Fora at 480 kW?

Vulco if you are adding power to an existing site — the module swap from 120 to 480 kW costs about 70% less than replacing the unit. Fora if the site is designed around many bays and you want up to 16 dispensers.
What is the maximum Fora output?
Fora spans 360–960 kW with up to 16 dispensers, so 480 kW sits near the low end of that system.
